Consequently, the uniform prior, Bayesian updates, and Bayes-optimal interpretation are heuristic rather than principled as claimed.

The belief construction appears to double-count the offline data. Every ensemble member is first trained on the complete dataset, after which prefixes of trajectories from that same dataset are reused to update model weights at rollout starting states. For a single fixed MuJoCo MDP, the posterior should already condition on all offline observations; resetting and locally reweighting models is closer to mixture-of-experts gating than inference over a fixed latent MDP.

It is unclear whether the deployed policy is actually Bayes-adaptive. The theory defines the policy and value functions on (s,h), or equivalently (s,b), but the experiments use the same feedforward architecture as the baselines, explicitly without history, and claim that deployment requires only policy-network inference. The paper never states whether b is an input or how it is updated at test time. If the policy receives only s, the main adaptive-policy claim does not hold.

The asserted near-Bayes-optimality is not established. The cited PUCT consistency result does not automatically cover the implemented algorithm, which uses constant widening parameters, hard action/state-child caps, learned proposal and value functions, and only 50 simulations. Moreover, optimizing an empirically penalized learned BAMDP cannot imply near-optimality in the true environment.

Algorithm 1 appears to sample reward and next state independently from two marginal ensemble mixtures, but then updates the belief using a same-model joint likelihood P_i(s'|s,a)R_i(r|s,a). A valid posterior-predictive transition requires a shared latent model index, or an explicitly specified joint model. Other important details, including the scalarization of the vector-valued uncertainty penalty and the search depth d_max, are also unclear.

The experiments do not cleanly isolate the contributions. BA-MBRL and BA-MCTS often use different numbers of epochs, MCTS adds many model queries, and the training curves rescale unequal epoch counts to a common axis. There is no compute- or model-query-matched non-search control, no policy-return ablation comparing adaptive and uniform ensemble weights, and no sensitivity analysis for search budget, depth, rho, or widening parameters.

The model-selection protocol creates a serious risk of offline-evaluation leakage. Many parameters are selected separately for each dataset, including lambda, K, H, N, exploration constants, child caps, and warm-up duration, while the true environment is evaluated after every epoch. The paper does not explain how these choices were made without using evaluation returns. Comparisons against externally reported baseline numbers therefore do not have comparable tuning budgets.

Statistical support is limited to three seeds, with no significance tests or uncertainty for many imported baselines. Some conclusions are stronger than the evidence: Table 1 appears to beat the best listed baseline on 8 of 12 tasks, not the claimed 9, and the average search improvement over BA-MBRL is modest and inconsistent across tasks.

The tokamak study is entirely conducted in a learned neural simulator that also generates the offline dataset; it is not real-device or genuinely real-world validation. The comparison includes only two baselines and does not address simulator bias, out-of-distribution safety, constraint violations, or the risks of applying the method to safety-critical plasma control.

The novelty relative to existing continuous belief-space/POMDP tree-search methods is not convincingly established. Continuous BAMCP is largely presented as explicit belief updates combined with existing DPW/PUCT machinery, while search-result distillation is also well established. A sharper comparison with POMCPOW and related continuous Bayesian planners, ideally with a new guarantee or controlled empirical evidence, is needed.
